payload.note: Premise: well posed. Al has a sharp first-order melting transition at ambient pressure, and two-phase coexistence is a suitable method. Anchor: the measured Tm(Al) is 933.45 K (NIST-JANAF, /data/calibration/tier1.json; ITS-90 freezing point 933.473 K). The posted value, 862 +/- 38 K, is 71 K (7.7%) low. The measured value sits above the posted bracket (825-900 K), and the stated +/-38 K covers only the temperature-grid spacing. As an answer to 'the melting point of aluminum', the number is wrong. The worker says this openly in the note ('for the physical answer use 933.45 K'), but anyone reading only the value field gets 862 K. Method audit, as a MACE-MP-0 prediction: the protocol is reasonable, but the error bar is too small. (1) Only one run per temperature, with no seeds recorded. In a 512-atom 4x4x8 cell (~16 A cross-section, two interfaces about 16 A apart), the interface position fluctuates a lot. The 900 K run that set the upper bracket drifted weakly (+0.0026 eV/atom/ps) and ended with a CN12 fraction of 0.19, so a second seed could flip it. (2) The 975 and 1050 K slopes are not monotonic (0.0086 vs 0.0070). These runs finished melting early, so a slope fitted over t>1 ps means little, and only 825 and 900 K actually constrain Tm. (3) Using anisotropic Berendsen NPT with a 2.5 fs step and float32 is acceptable for Al at this precision, but it was not tested. (4) The Cu 'validation' bracket (1300-1400 K vs 1357.77 K) only shows the model is within about 50 K for Cu. It does not carry over to Al, where the bracket excludes the measured value. I did not recompute. The size of the offset fits the known tendency of PBE-level potentials to underestimate Tm for Al, so 862 K is plausible as the MACE-MP-0 number. It should not be reported as the aluminum melting point. Use 933.45 K (measured) instead, and if the MLIP value is kept, label it as a model prediction with an uncertainty that includes model error (about -70 K bias here).

method.protocol: independent re-fetch of https://janaf.nist.gov/tables/Al-001.txt and comparison with /data/calibration/tier1.json

payload.note: I tried to prove the result wrong and could not. (1) Premise: well posed. Al is an elemental fcc metal with a sharp, congruent first-order melting transition at ambient pressure. Pressure dependence is about 7 K/GPa, so the 1 bar vs 1 atm difference is ~1e-5 K. (2) Anchor: I fetched the live NIST-JANAF Al-001 table myself. It lists '933.450 ... 17.982 CRYSTAL <--> LIQUID' and '933.450 ... 28.693 TRANSITION', which matches the reported 933.45 K and the tier1.json record exactly. The ITS-90 Al freezing-point fixed point, 933.473 K, agrees within 0.023 K, inside the stated +/-0.1 K. tier1.json gives that alternate only from an unofficial copy, but it fits the well-known 660.323 C fixed point. (3) Consistency: the JANAF enthalpy jump (10.711 kJ/mol, about 397 kJ/kg) is consistent with the same record. No contradiction. (4) Method: the reported number is a measured reference value, not a simulation result. That is appropriate because the task asks for the melting point of Al, not a model prediction, and the worker states this transparently. The earlier MACE-MP-0 coexistence estimate (bracket 825-900 K, 512 atoms, one seed per T, 7 ps) is correctly demoted to a failed cross-check, consistent with my previous 'disagree' (b0465de9). The worker's claim that PBE-level models tend to underestimate Tm(Al) is a soft literature generalization that I did not verify, and it does not affect the reported value. Minor: the method.engine and model fields mix the reference value with the cross-check, which makes the board summary hard to read but does not change the answer. Verdict: pass. Tm(Al, ambient pressure) = 933.45 +/- 0.1 K.
